newsitem.title: USA: Former Orange County treasurer awaits sentencing.
newsitem.headline: Former Orange County treasurer awaits sentencing.

text.p: The former treasurer of California's Orange County was set to be sentenced Tuesday for his role in the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history.
Robert Citron, widely blamed for the county's financial crisis, pleaded guilty in April 1995 to six felonies, including making untrue statements in the sale of securities and misusing public funds.
Citron, 71, who has been cooperating with prosecutors, faces up to 14 years in prison.

Superior Court Judge J. Stephen Czuleger heard testimony Monday from Citron's friends, who warned that sending the ex-treasurer to jail could kill him, and psychologists, who described Citron as mentally impaired.
Citron's sentencing hearing was scheduled to continue in Santa Ana on Tuesday. At the end of the court session, the judge was expected to hand the ex-treasurer his sentence.

Orange County filed for bankruptcy protection from creditors on Dec. 6, 1994, after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. It was the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history. The county emerged from bankruptcy last June.
Orange County District Attorney Michael Capizzi has recommended that Citron be sentenced to seven years in prison and fined $400,000.

"We recognise that Mr. Citron may have certain brain dysfunctions, but that doesn't change the fact that he understood the crimes he committed," Assistant District Attoney Matthew Anderson said. "He knew it was wrong and he did it anyways."
Citron attorney David Wiechert has called the district attorney's sentencing recommendation "incredibly harsh." He argued that Citron has already "paid dearly" for his crimes.
Wiechert has painted a tragic portrait of his client. Psychologists testified Monday in court that Citron suffered from brain impairments.
Wiechert said Citron's psychological "deficits" had rendered him susceptible to advice from "trusted" counsellors, such as investment giant Merrill Lynch & Co.

"He relied primarily on his closest advisers, assistant treasurers with college degrees who were CPAs (certified public accountants), and the largest brokerage firm in America," Wiechert argued in court papers prepared for the hearing. "In the end, his mind and his counsellors failed him."
Merrill Lynch has said Citron was an experienced and sophisticated treasurer who made his own investment decisions.
